back: The study of history of life forms on earth — the story of the origin and evolution of biodiversity, set against the evolution of earth and of the universe itself.
The idea that units of life called spores were transferred to different planets, including earth, from outer space. Still a favourite idea for some astronomers.
The old theory that life arose from decaying and rotting matter such as straw or mud. Dismissed once and for all by Louis Pasteur's experiments with pre-sterilised flasks.
The formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents, preceding the formation of life. Proposed by Oparin and Haldane and supported by Miller's experiment.
The version that the first form of life arose slowly through evolutionary forces from non-living molecules. Accepted by the majority of scientists.
Electric discharge passed through a closed flask of CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 degrees Celsius produced amino acids. Similar experiments produced sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats.
The claim that all organisms were created as such, that diversity has always been the same and will stay the same, and that the earth is about 4000 years old. Challenged in the nineteenth century.
The sail ship on which Charles Darwin made his round-the-world voyage, from whose observations he concluded that life forms share similarities with each other and with extinct forms.
Darwin's mechanism of evolution: those better fit in an environment leave more progeny, survive more, and are therefore selected by nature.
Reproductive fitness — the ability to leave more progeny. It refers ultimately and only to reproduction, not to strength or size.
Remains of hard parts of life-forms found in rocks. Different-aged rock sediments contain fossils of different life-forms, which is the palaeontological evidence for evolution.
Structures with a similar anatomical plan but different functions, produced by divergent evolution and indicating common ancestry. Example: forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and human.
Structures that are anatomically dissimilar but perform the same function, produced by convergent evolution. Example: wings of a butterfly and of a bird.
The same basic structure developing along different directions because of adaptation to different needs — the basis of homology.
Different structures evolving for the same function, and hence showing similarity. Similar habitat selects similar adaptive features in different groups of organisms.
Evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from one point and radiating into other habitats. Examples: Darwin's finches, Australian marsupials.

Evolution driven by human action, such as the selection of resistant varieties by excess use of herbicides and pesticides, or of resistant microbes by antibiotics. It appears in months or years, not centuries.
Evolution driven by use and disuse of organs, with acquired characters passed to the next generation — his giraffe example. Nobody believes this conjecture any more.
The term deVries used for speciation by a single step large mutation. Mutations are random and directionless, unlike the small directional variations Darwin described.

Allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation; the gene pool remains constant, which is called genetic equilibrium. For two alleles, p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1.
The total genes and their alleles in a population. The Hardy-Weinberg principle says this pool remains a constant.

A change in allele frequency that occurs by chance. When the drifted sample differs so much that it becomes a different species, the original population is called the founders and the effect is the founder effect.
The effect produced when a drifted sample of a population becomes so different in allele frequency that it forms a different species, with the original drifted population as the founders.
Stabilising (more individuals acquire the mean value), directional (more acquire a value other than the mean) and disruptive (more acquire peripheral values at both ends of the distribution).
A fish caught in South Africa in 1938, thought to be extinct. These lobefins evolved into the first amphibians, which lived on both land and water.
Primates existing about 15 mya. Both were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Ramapithecus was more man-like, Dryopithecus more ape-like.
The first human-like being, a hominid, of about 2 mya. Brain capacity 650 to 800 cc; probably did not eat meat.
The stage revealed by fossils discovered in Java in 1891, about 1.5 mya. Large brain of about 900 cc; probably ate meat.
Brain size 1400 cc; lived in the near east and central Asia between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years back. Used hides to protect the body and buried the dead.
Pre-historic cave paintings about 18,000 years old, in Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh.
